facts.text: The word origami comes from two Japanese words: ori (fold) and kami (paper).
Paper was expensive in early Japan, so folding was at first limited to ceremonies and formal gift wrapping.
At Shinto weddings, folded paper butterflies decorate bottles of sake (rice wine).
When paper became cheaper during the Edo period (1603 to 1868), folding spread to toys, gift wrap and geometry lessons for children.
In the twentieth century Akira Yoshizawa helped raise paper folding to a fine art and created many new models.
Yoshizawa developed a system of dotted lines, dashes and arrows for folding instructions that is still the basis of origami diagrams today.
Some leading origami designers, such as former laser physicist Robert Lang, use mathematics to design very complex models, folding them from a single uncut square of paper.
Japanese astrophysicist Koryo Miura described the Miura fold, which lets a flat sheet fold up compactly and open in one motion.
The Miura fold was used to pack the solar panels of Japan's Space Flyer Unit satellite, launched in 1995.
NASA's James Webb Space Telescope was launched on 25 December 2021 folded origami-style to fit inside its rocket, then unfolded in space.
Webb's sunshield is about the size of a tennis court and was folded around the telescope's mirrors during launch.
Engineers at the University of Oxford designed an origami stent graft, a tube for treating blocked or weakened vessels, that folds small for delivery and expands where it is needed.
